analysis.one_liner: Lets investors subtract inflation from taxable gains on stocks and business assets held over three years.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 90 House sponsors and cosponsors, all Republicans, but the Ways and Means Committee never took it up, and it died without a vote when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change how capital-gains tax is calculated for assets like corporate stock and business property held for more than three years. Today, tax is owed on the full gain between purchase price and sale price, including the part that is just inflation. This bill would raise the purchase-price figure by the inflation rate, so tax would be due only on gains above inflation. It would also extend that treatment to mutual funds, real estate investment trusts, partnerships, and short sales.
analysis.who_benefits: Households and businesses that hold taxable, appreciated assets — stocks, real estate, and business property — for more than three years. Because the benefit only reaches people who actually owe capital-gains tax on assets held in taxable accounts (money in 401(k)s and IRAs is already tax-sheltered, so no adjustment applies there), the gains would flow mainly to higher-income investors, business owners selling appreciated property, and real estate investors.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Investors and owners of appreciated assets

how_it_helps.text: Raises the taxable "basis" (the original purchase price) of corporate stock and tangible business property by the inflation rate, measured with the GDP deflator, for assets held more than three years, so tax is due only on gains above inflation [S2][S3].

Extends the inflation adjustment through regulated investment companies (mutual funds), real estate investment trusts, partnerships, S corporations, and short sales, with rules to keep the benefit from reaching corporate shareholders indirectly [S2][S3].
Applies only to assets acquired after December 31, 2007, and only where the taxpayer has written documentation of the original purchase price [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury, and ultimately general taxpayers, who would receive less revenue because inflation-driven gains would no longer be taxed. Taxpayers would also face added recordkeeping, since the adjustment requires written proof of the original purchase price.

drawbacks.text: The bill reduces federal revenue by untaxing the inflation portion of investment gains; that revenue would otherwise be available for public spending or would have to be replaced by taxes on other income, including wages [S2][S3].
The benefit is concentrated: it reaches only taxpayers who owe capital-gains tax on assets held outside retirement accounts, while the revenue cost falls on everyone.

Indexing basis also enlarges deductible losses on inflation-adjusted sales; the bill responds by converting what would be ordinary losses into less-valuable capital losses, adding complexity for taxpayers with losses [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The underlying idea has a fair argument: taxing a gain that is only inflation taxes money the investor never really made. But the way this bill is written, the benefits go to whoever holds appreciated taxable assets — a group concentrated at the top of the income scale — while the cost is spread across all taxpayers as lost revenue. It is a real tax cut, not a subsidy scam, but it is not aimed at working people, and the bill never got far enough for Congress to weigh that tradeoff in the open.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Ways and Means Committee on the day it was filed, and the committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mike Pence introduced the bill on March 1, 2007, joined by Rep. Eric Cantor, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means [S5][S3].
Eighty-eight House Republicans cosponsored, bringing total sponsorship to 90; every sponsor and cosponsor was a Republican [S4].
The action history shows no activity beyond the referral for the remainder of the 110th Congress, which ended January 3, 2009 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal Treasury kept the revenue the bill would have given up, and investors who already held assets kept the existing capital-gains rules unchanged. No one new gained ground; the main effect of the bill dying was that a tax cut for asset holders never happened.

for.name: Rep. Mike Pence
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Capital Gains Inflation Relief Act of 2007 on March 1, 2007.

for.name: Rep. Eric Cantor
for.what_they_did: Joined Pence in introducing the bill, which was filed "for himself and Mr. Cantor."

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; Democratic-controlled in the 110th Congress
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill on the day of introduction and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 90 sponsors and cosponsors were House Republicans; no Democrat cosponsored, and the Democratic majority that controlled the committee and floor schedule took no action on it.

industries.industry: Wealthy households holding appreciated taxable assets
industries.note: These taxpayers would pay tax only on gains above inflation on stock and business property held over three years. The benefit goes to those who owe capital-gains tax outside retirement accounts — concentrated among higher-income households — while the lost revenue falls on all taxpayers.

industries.industry: Mutual fund companies and their taxable shareholders
industries.note: The bill includes detailed rules letting mutual funds pass the inflation adjustment through to shareholders, cutting tax for investors in taxable accounts. Investors saving through tax-sheltered retirement accounts would see no change.
REIT shares and business real estate qualify for the inflation adjustment, with special ratio rules for REITs, reducing tax on long-held property sales. The revenue cost is shared by all taxpayers.

Owners selling a business or its tangible property after three years would be taxed only on the real gain, not inflation. This narrows but does not eliminate the revenue the Treasury collects on such sales.
